newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-KNICKS SUSPENSIONS STAND AFTER LEGAL CHALLENGE DENIED.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-KNICKS SUSPENSIONS STAND AFTER LEGAL CHALLENGE DENIED.

text.p: The New York Knicks and their fans got bad news hours before a key playoff game Friday when a U.S. District Court judge upheld the league's suspension of five Knicks and one Miami Heat player.
Judge Jed Rakoff denied the NBA Players Association a temporary restraining order against some of the suspensions, ruling that the commissioner's office held the exclusive right to issue discipline.

As a result of the ruling, the Knicks will be without All-Star centre Patrick Ewing and starting guard Allan Houston -- the team's two leading scorers -- and backup point guard Charlie Ward for Friday's Game Six.
In addition, New York starting forward Larry Johnson and guard John Starks -- the league's Sixth Man Award winner -- must sit out the following game.
Heat forward P.J. Brown was given a two-game suspension for instigating an ugly brawl near the end of Wednesday's game in Miami and will miss the rest of the Eastern Conference semifinal series.
Because teams must dress no less than nine players for playoff games, the New York suspensions were split up over two games.
"We think he's wrong, we think it's unfair to the players, we think it's unfair to the fans of the team," Players Association (NBPA) attorney Jeffery Kessler said of the ruling.
The penalties handed out by NBA discipline chief Rod Thorne were the harshest ever issued by the NBA in the playoffs.

The melee began when Brown took exception to the way Ward tried to block him out while awaiting a rebound after a free throw. Brown picked up the much smaller Ward and slammed him to the floor and players from both teams went at each other.
Players who were already on the court and took part in the brawl, except for Brown and Ward, were not punished.
The union challenged only the suspensions to Ewing, Houston, Johnson and Starks, who were punished for leaving the team's bench during the brawl near the New York bench.
The NBA based its sanctions on a strict interpretation of its rule, which says any player leaving the bench area during an altercation must receive at least a one-game suspension.
NBPA executive director Billy Hunter was seeking a temporary restraining order, contending that the league acted improperly "in suspending those players who left the bench to act as peacemakers."
The union contended that the rules the NBA used to determine the punishments were not collectively bargained and therefore arbitrary and subject to arbitration.
The judge expressed sympathy toward the players, agreeing that they would suffer irreparable harm by missing the crucial playoff games.
However, legally he felt that the issue of the NBA's right to impose swift discipline for on-court behaviour was not subject to arbitration, according to the Collective Bargaining Agreement.
The judge called language giving the NBA Commissioner's office exclusive control of discipline for on-court behaviour "so plain, so clear and so unequivocal."
Particularly galling to the Knicks and their fans was the suspension of Ewing, who left the bench but had no part in the fracas, watching it from a distance after one of his teammates stopped him.
"You have to play with the circumstance that are dealt to you," said Knicks head coach Jeff Van Gundy. "We got nine guys tonight, we believe we can win with nine guys."
